answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Cicero really did write this — the Latin “Si hortum in bibliotheca habes, deerit nihil” is a genuine line from his letter to Varro (Ad Familiares 9.4.1, 46 BC). But the famous English one-liner is a loose paraphrase, not a standard translation: the Loeb edition (W. Glynn Williams, 1928) renders it “If you have a garden in your library, we shall have all we want,” and Cicero wrote of a garden within a library, not a garden and a library.

source.excerpt: Si hortum in bibliotheca habes, deerit nihil. — “If you have a garden in your library, we shall have all we want.”
trail: The Latin original, “Si hortum in bibliotheca habes, deerit nihil,” is confirmed in the standard text of Ad Familiares 9.4.
The scholarly Loeb translation by W. Glynn Williams (1928) reads “If you have a garden in your library, we shall have all we want,” per WIST’s cited entry.
Wikiquote lists the Latin as authentic but pairs it with the popular paraphrase “If you have a garden and a library, you have everything you need.”
source.excerptNote: Cicero is arranging a visit with the scholar Varro: the garden feeds the body, the library the mind. The remark is about what would make their meeting place complete — not a universal maxim for a well-lived life.
source.rightsNote: The ancient Latin is public domain, and the 1928 Loeb translation shown for context is itself old enough to be public domain. But the exact wording displayed here — “If you have a garden and a library, you have everything you need” — is an anonymous modern paraphrase with no identifiable translator and no documented pre-1931 appearance, so we assert no copyright status for it.

author.name: Marcus Tullius Cicero
author.heading: Marcus Tullius Cicero
author.bio: Cicero (106–43 BC) was Rome’s foremost orator and a prolific writer on rhetoric, politics, and philosophy. The garden-and-library remark comes from his vast personal correspondence — the Epistulae ad Familiares — here in a warm note to the polymath scholar Marcus Terentius Varro, arranging where the two learned friends might best meet and talk.

misattribution.heading: A real quote, a reshaped line
misattribution.intro: This is not a case of a fake Cicero quote — he genuinely wrote it. The problem is the wording: the popular English quietly changes both the sense and the grammar of what he actually said.

items.why: Cicero wrote “hortum in bibliotheca” — a garden in (or within) a library. The popular line turns that into a garden and a library, two separate things. The scholarly Loeb translation keeps the original: “If you have a garden in your library…”

In the letter, “deerit nihil” (“nothing will be lacking”) is about what would make Cicero’s meeting with Varro complete — Loeb: “we shall have all we want.” Quote collections such as libquotes recast it as a universal life maxim, “you have everything you need.”

misattribution.truthLine: The sentiment is authentically Cicero’s, from Ad Familiares 9.4 — but the exact famous English line is a paraphrase, not a real translation.

context.heading: Why the garden and the library
lead: The Roman garden was not merely ornamental. For an educated Roman like Cicero or Varro it was a place for walking, thinking, and philosophical conversation — an outdoor extension of the study. Read that way, his line to Varro is less “own a garden and own a library” and more “set a library among the greenery and there is nothing left to wish for.”

That is exactly the nuance the popular paraphrase flattens. It is a lovely sentiment either way — which is why it endures on tote bags and bookshop walls — but the crisp modern maxim is a descendant of Cicero’s words, not a transcript of them.
detailsBody: The letter belongs to a group Cicero wrote to Varro in 46 BC, during Caesar’s dictatorship, when both men had withdrawn somewhat from public life into study. The tone throughout is that of two scholars planning how best to spend their time together.
context.pull: A garden in a library — not a garden and a library.
